questions.prompt: What is the intent of the Command pattern?

options.text: Encapsulate a request as an object so it can be parameterized, queued, logged, and undone
Pass a request along a chain of handlers
Provide a simplified interface to a subsystem

questions.explanation: Command turns a request into an object. Passing along a chain = Chain of Responsibility; simplifying = Facade; families = Abstract Factory.

questions.prompt: Match each Command role to its responsibility.

pairs.right: Represents the action, usually with execute()/undo()
Triggers the command without knowing its details

questions.explanation: The invoker calls execute(); the concrete command tells the receiver what to do; the client wires them together.

questions.prompt: Which capabilities does turning an action into a Command object unlock? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Command enables undo/redo, queuing, and logging/replay. Single-instance guarantees are Singleton's job.

questions.prompt: Which method typically accompanies execute() to support undo?

options.text: undo(), which reverses the effect of execute()

questions.explanation: A symmetric undo() reverses execute(); a history of commands enables undo/redo.

questions.prompt: In TypeScript, when is a plain function enough instead of a full Command object?

options.text: For fire-and-forget actions that don't need undo, queuing, logging, or serialization
Never — Command always requires a class
Only when there is exactly one receiver

questions.explanation: First-class functions cover simple actions; the object form pays off when you need Command's extra powers.

questions.prompt: Which pattern is often paired with Command to implement undo?

options.text: Memento — it captures and restores an object's prior state

questions.explanation: Memento snapshots state so a command's undo can roll back to the earlier state.
